chunks: Al-Husayn ibn Muhammad, from Ahmad ibn Ishaq, and Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, all together, from Bakr ibn Muhammad al-Azdi, who said:

I entered upon Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) and with me was Ali ibn Abdul Aziz. So he said to me: 'Who is this?' So I said, 'A slave of ours'. So he said: 'Have you emancipated him, or his father?' So I said, 'But his father'. So he said: 'This one is not your slave. This is your brother, and a son of your uncle. But rather, the slave is the one upon whom the bounty flows. So when it flowed upon his father, so he is your brother, and a son of your uncle'.

key_terms.أَعْتَقْتُمُوهُ: You have emancipated him (past tense, referring to the slave himself).
key_terms.النِّعْمَةُ: The bounty/favor; here referring to the grace of emancipation or status elevation.
key_terms.مَوْلًى: Slave or freedman; in this context, refers to a client or one under guardianship, redefined by the Imam based on lineage and favor.

ai.seo_question: What is the status of a son if his father was emancipated in Shia jurisprudence?
ai.summary: This hadith from *Al-Kafi* elucidates the Shia jurisprudential distinction between *mawla* (client/slave) and *akh* (brother) by linking social status to the lineage of emancipation rather than mere ownership. Imam al-Sadiq (peace be upon him) establishes that if the father was freed, the son inherits that status of freedom and kinship, thereby redefining the term *mawla* as one who has received the favor of emancipation through their ancestor. This reflects the broader Shia emphasis on the spiritual and social elevation of the freed and their descendants within the community.
